procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but implied to be a trial court in Patna, given the Patna High Court's involvement in the first appeal.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 31st January, 1969 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 254 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Mallabir, Dasrath, Kasim and Mahadeo appealed to the Patna High Court. The High Court dismissed their appeal. The High Court upheld the conviction of Mahadeo and Kasim under sections 120B and 201 of the Indian Penal Code and the sentences awarded to them.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Mallabir, Dasrath, Kasim and Mahadeo, the four convicted accused, appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave.

decision.appeal_result: Appeal of Dasrath and Kasltu is allowed. The appeal of Mahabir and Mahadeo is dismissed to the extent indicated.
decision.conviction_status: Conviction of Dasrath and Kasltu is set aside. Conviction of Mahabir and Mahadeo for offences under section 120B Indian Penal Code is set aside. Conviction of Mahabir for offences under sections 302 and 201 Indian Penal Code is maintained. Conviction of Mahadeo for offence under section 201 Indian Penal Code is maintained.
decision.sentence_status: Sentence of Mahabir for offences under sections 302 and 201 Indian Penal Code is maintained. Sentence of Mahadeo for offence under section 201 Indian Penal Code is maintained.

issue.issue_text: Whether the statements made by two appellants to the police, on which the prosecution relied, were admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act.

facts: The prosecution relied on statements made by two appellants, Kasim and Mahadeo, to the police at the police station on September 18, 1963.
law: Under section 26 of the Indian Evidence Act, a confession made by a person in police custody is generally inadmissible.
Section 27 of the Evidence Act provides an exception to this rule, allowing a statement to be admitted if it results in the discovery of any incriminating material.
application: The court examined the facts of the case and found there was no evidence to show that the statements made by the two appellants led to the discovery of any incriminating material.

The court explicitly stated, "There is nothing in the present case to show that the statements... resulted in the discovery of any incriminating material as may make them admissible under section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act."
reasoning.conclusion: Because the statements did not lead to the discovery of any incriminating material, the condition required for the exception under section 27 was not met. Therefore, the court ruled that the statements were inadmissible and must be excluded from consideration.

issue.issue_text: Whether the first appellant was responsible for the death of the deceased based on the circumstances and evidence on record.

facts: The trial court and the High Court, based on the materials on record, had already found that the first appellant was responsible for the death of the deceased by poisoning.
The appellant's counsel argued that the evidence did not establish that the first appellant caused the death, nor was it proven that the death was homicidal rather than natural.
law: The Court held that a conviction can be based on circumstantial evidence, even in the absence of direct proof.

If circumstantial evidence is so decisive that the court can unhesitatingly conclude that death was a result of poison administered by the accused (even if the poison itself is not detected), then a conviction can be upheld.
application: The Court found that the circumstances of the case and the evidence on record clearly pointed to the first appellant's responsibility for the death.
The Court applied the principle regarding decisive circumstantial evidence to the first appellant's case.
Based on this, the Court found no reason to interfere with the findings of the two lower courts that the death was not natural but homicidal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court confirmed the conviction of the first appellant, holding that the circumstantial evidence was decisive enough to establish that he was responsible for the homicidal death of the deceased by poisoning.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution had proved its case against two of the appellants.

facts: The appellants Dasrath and Kasim were convicted by the trial court and the High Court.
The prosecution relied on statements made by the two appellants to the police.
law: The Court referenced Section 27 of the Evidence Act, which allows statements made to police to be admitted as evidence if they result in the discovery of an incriminating fact.
application: The Court found that there was "no cogent evidence on the record" to prove that the appellant Dasrath was present at the scene of the crime.

The Court also found that the statements made by the two appellants (Dasrath and Kasim) to the police did not result in the discovery of any incriminating evidence, which would have been necessary to make them admissible under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution had not proven its case against the appellants Dasrath and Kasim. Therefore, the Court allowed their appeal, set aside their convictions, and acquitted them.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the statements made by two appellants to the police, on which the prosecution relied, were admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act.
appellant_arguments: The statements made to the police did not lead to the discovery of any incriminating material and therefore are not admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act and must be excluded from consideration.
respondent_arguments: The statements made by the appellants to the police were admissible under the provisions of section 27 of the Evidence Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the first appellant was responsible for the death of the deceased based on the circumstances and evidence on record.
appellant_arguments: The material on record does not establish that the first appellant (Mahabir) caused the death of the deceased.
It has not been proven that the death was homicidal and not natural.
respondent_arguments: The circumstances of the case and the evidence on record clearly point out that the first appellant was responsible for the death of the deceased.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution had proved its case against two of the appellants.
appellant_arguments: There is no cogent evidence on the record to show that one of the appellants (Dasrath) was present at the scene of the crime.
No case has been proved against two of the appellants, and their conviction should be set aside.
respondent_arguments: The case against the appellants was sufficiently proven to warrant a conviction.

cases.principle: The bar of inadmissibility of statements made to the police under Section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure operates not only on statements of witnesses but also on those of the accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The rule in section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is not applicable to statements falling within the provisions of clause (i) of section 32 of the Evidence Act or to affect the provisions of section 27 of that Act.
obiter: The exercise of extra-ordinary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution is not justifiable in criminal cases unless exceptional and special circumstances are shown to exist or that substantial and grave injustice has been done.

The pathologist's part in the diagnosis of poisoning is secondary, and several poisons, particularly of the synthetic hypnotics and vegetable alkaloids groups, do not leave any characteristic signs which can be noticed on post-mortem examination.
Not much help can be derived from a cited case if there is no parallel between the facts of the two cases.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that while statements made by the appellants to the police were inadmissible under Section 27 of the Evidence Act for failing to lead to the discovery of any incriminating material, the case against the first appellant was proven by decisive circumstantial evidence. This evidence was sufficient to unhesitatingly hold that the death was a homicide by poisoning committed by him. Conversely, the court determined that the prosecution had failed to prove its case against two other appellants, leading to their acquittal.
legal_tests_applied: For a statement to the police to be admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act, it must result in the discovery of incriminating material.

If circumstantial evidence, in the absence of direct proof, is so decisive that the Court can unhesitatingly hold that the death was a result of the administration of poison and that the poison must have been administered by the accused person, then a conviction can be rested on it.

The exercise of extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution is not justifiable in criminal cases unless exceptional and special circumstances are shown to exist or that substantial and grave injustice has been done.
why_appellant_lost: The court found no cogent ground to interfere with the findings of the two lower courts that the death of the deceased was not natural but homicidal.
The circumstances of the case and the evidence on record clearly pointed out that the first appellant was responsible for the death of the deceased and that the death was caused by poisoning.
why_respondent_won: The statements made by two appellants to the police were inadmissible because there was nothing to show that they resulted in the discovery of any incriminating material as may make them admissible under section 27 of the Evidence Act.
The court was of the opinion that no case had been proved against the appellants Dasrath and Kasim.
